summary: I and ME are the same sign in ASL: an index finger pointing to or touching your chest. The English word changes; the sign does not.
steps: Point your index finger at the center of your chest, or touch it.
That's it. For emphasis, touch firmly.
Use it for both 'I' and 'me': I HUNGRY, HELP ME (HELP moving toward you).
note: Some signed-English systems teach an I handshape (pinky up) on the chest for 'I.' That's not ASL. In ASL, the index-finger point is I and ME both, and native signers rarely use the pinky version.
mistakes: Using the pinky-up I handshape. That's borrowed from signed English, not ASL.
Looking for a separate ME sign. There isn't one.

faq.q: Why is 'me' the same as 'I' in ASL?
faq.a: Because ASL pronouns are pointing. Pointing at yourself means yourself, whether English would say I or me. The grammar role comes from word order and verb direction, not from a different pronoun.
MY uses a flat hand on the chest instead of a pointing finger. The rule: index finger for the pronoun, flat hand for the possessive.
